play_commands.title: Exploring: Phoebe Bridgers
play_commands.narrative: Perfect timing: “Lost Boys” turned out to be the lead single for Lost Weekend, Bridgers’ first solo album since 2020’s Punisher — and it dropped today. Her longtime producers Tony Berg and Ethan Gruska are back, now joined behind the boards by Jack Antonoff and Alex G, while the single alone stacks Julien Baker, Lucy Dacus and Caroline Shaw on vocals, Chris Thile on mandolin, Rob Moose on strings and Bright Eyes’ Nate Walcott on trumpets. This card traces that collaboration web — boygenius, Better Oblivion Community Center, and the producers’ own records — sparked by June’s first spin of the single.

items.label: 💿 Stranger in the Alps (2017) — Phoebe Bridgers
items.note: ✨ New to you — her 2017 debut, where the Berg/Gruska production partnership heard on 'Lost Boys' first formed (Tape Op: Berg brought Gruska in to co-produce).

items.note: ✨ New to you — co-producer Ethan Gruska's own solo album; Bridgers returns the favor with a guest vocal on 'Enough for Now'.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Jungle
play_commands.narrative: Jungle are the London neo-soul/nu-disco trio built by Josh Lloyd-Watson and Tom McFarland — next-door neighbours since age nine who hid behind the aliases 'J' and 'T' on their Mercury-shortlisted XL debut, now joined full-time by Lydia Kitto and running their own Caiola label. 'Someday, Somewhere' is the third single from their fifth album Sunshine, released today (Aug 14, 2026). Their collaboration web runs wide: guest spots from Bas, Priya Ragu, Erick the Architect, Channel Tres and Roots Manuva, remixes for Taylor Swift and Brittany Howard, and a production credit on Le Sserafim's 'Come Over' — plus a buried pre-fame shoegaze band and a 2025 side project, both below. (Sparked by today's 'Someday, Somewhere' spin.)

play_commands.title: Going deeper: A Certain Ratio
play_commands.narrative: Deep dive 2 — the first card told the Factory story, so this one follows the family tree out of it. When founders Simon Topping and Peter Terrell quit in late '82, Topping formed proto-house act T-Coy with Quando Quango's Mike Pickering; keyboardist Andy Connell left in '85 to launch Swing Out Sister (whose Corinne Drewery repaid the favour by guesting on Force); and Martin Moscrop's jazz-funk side band Swamp Children became Kalima, sending sax player Tony Quigley the other way into ACR, where he still plays. The band's own buried chapter is the A&M years — Good Together (1989) and acr:mcr (1990), the big-budget records that pulled Haçienda club kids onboard before Rob Gretton's Rob's Records took them in — and running through it all is the late Denise Johnson, Screamadelica's gold-plated voice, an ACR member from 1989 whose lone solo album arrived posthumously in 2020.

suggestions.genre_source: web search snippets: Wikipedia infobox 'post-punk, funk, new wave, avant-funk, dance-punk, dance-rock'; Guardian 'pioneers of punk funk'

items.label: 1982 (2023) — A Certain Ratio
items.note: ✨ New to you — the one studio album the first card skipped: named for their Sextet year, the current six-piece revisits that era's Latin percussion with modern electronics, made entirely on their own terms for Mute.

items.label: Good Together (1989) — A Certain Ratio
items.note: ✨ New to you — the buried A&M major-label chapter: recorded after they built their own SoundStation studio in Manchester, with singles "The Big E" and "Backs to the Wall" grazing the UK chart.

items.label: acr:mcr (1990) — A Certain Ratio
items.note: ✨ New to you — the record that pulled a new generation of dance/club fans to ACR, with "Won't Stop Loving You" (their only UK Top 60 single) — right before A&M dropped them and Rob Gretton's Rob's Records picked them up.

items.label: It's Better to Travel (1987) — Swing Out Sister
items.note: ✨ New to you — keyboardist Andy Connell left ACR in 1985 and took punk-funk sophistication to the top: this debut hit UK #1 with "Breakout"; singer Corinne Drewery repaid the favour guesting on ACR's Force.

items.label: Pigs & Battleships (1985) — Quando Quango
items.note: ✨ New to you — Factory label-mates and the missing link in the T-Coy story: Mike Pickering's Latin-dance outfit, before he formed T-Coy with ex-ACR frontman Simon Topping and then M People.

items.label: Night Time Shadows + Singles (1986) — Kalima
items.note: ✨ New to you — Factory's jazz-funk spin-off begun by ACR's Martin Moscrop as Swamp Children; the bands swapped members for years, and Kalima sax player Tony Quigley crossed over to ACR for good. (Spotify credits it under 'Kali Ma'.)

items.label: Where Does It Go (2020) — Denise Johnson
items.note: ✨ New to you — ACR's vocalist from 1989 until her death in 2020, and the voice of Manchester's dancefloors (Primal Scream's Screamadelica, New Order): her only solo album, released posthumously — mostly acoustic, quietly devastating.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Happy Mondays
play_commands.narrative: Happy Mondays were Factory Records' unruly id — signed to Tony Wilson's label after a demo tape reached a Haçienda DJ, they fused indie guitars with house, funk and northern soul into the Madchester 'baggy' sound (explored here by direct request). Their producer lineage is remarkable: John Cale on the 1987 debut, Joy Division's Martin Hannett on Bummed, and DJ Paul Oakenfold with Steve Osborne on the platinum Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches — for AllMusic the peak of the whole movement. The infamously debauched Barbados sessions for Yes Please!, produced by Talking Heads' Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth, helped bankrupt Factory; Shaun Ryder and Bez walked out of the wreckage into Black Grape.

suggestions.genre_source: web search snippet: Wikipedia infobox — 'Baggy, alternative dance, post-punk, Madchester, neo-psychedelia'

items.label: Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches (1990) — Happy Mondays
items.note: 🔁 1 play (a lone Step On, last July) — Paul Oakenfold & Steve Osborne's dancefloor production made this the baggy movement's platinum peak; AllMusic called it 'a celebratory collage of sex, drugs, and dead-end jobs'.

items.label: Bummed (1988) — Happy Mondays
items.note: ✨ New to you — produced by Joy Division's Martin Hannett as ecstasy hit Manchester; the album that dragged acid house's Second Summer of Love into rock, with the proto-baggy singles Wrote for Luck and Lazyitis.

items.label: Unknown Pleasures (1979) — Joy Division
items.note: ✨ New to you — same producer as Bummed: Martin Hannett, whose cavernous studio sound built Factory Records a decade before he wired up the Mondays.

items.label: It's Great When You're Straight... Yeah (1995) — Black Grape
items.note: ✨ New to you — Shaun Ryder and Bez's post-Mondays band went straight to UK #1 with this debut; looser, funnier and funkier than anything after Factory collapsed.

items.label: Tom Tom Club (1981) — Tom Tom Club
items.note: 🔁 5 plays, last 5 days ago — Chris Frantz & Tina Weymouth produced the Mondays' Yes Please! at Eddy Grant's Barbados studio; this is the elastic funk playbook they brought with them.

items.label: Squirrel And G-Man Twenty Four Hour Party People Plastic Face Carnt Smile (White Out) (1987) — Happy Mondays
items.note: ✨ New to you — the scrappy debut, produced by the Velvet Underground's John Cale; its title gave the Factory Records film 24 Hour Party People its name.

items.label: The Stone Roses (1989) — The Stone Roses
items.note: 🔁 3 plays, last Nov — Madchester's other pillar, from the same Haçienda scene with the opposite temperament: the Roses reached for the sublime while the Mondays reached for the gutter.

items.label: The Stone Roses · Happy Mondays · The Charlatans — Madchester Best Of (playlist)
items.note: ✨ Baggy scene catch-all — Mondays alongside Stone Roses, The Charlatans, Ian Brown and Primal Scream; the whole Haçienda-era sound in one sitting.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Kacey Musgraves
play_commands.narrative: Middle of Nowhere (2026) — her seventh album and first on the revived Lost Highway label — is Musgraves' homecoming: written during the longest single stretch of her adult life back in small-town Texas, and the most classically country she's ever sounded, with four different pedal steel players credited. It reunites both of her creative circles at once: Golden Hour producers Daniel Tashian & Ian Fitchuk behind the board, and the Same Trailer-era writing crew (Shane McAnally, Luke Laird, Josh Osborne, Brandy Clark) who penned 'Dry Spell' with her. The guest list settles old scores and walks the Texas-Mexico fence line: Willie Nelson croons over cumbia on 'Uncertain, TX', Miranda Lambert buries their 13-year 'Mama's Broken Heart' feud in the norteno waltz 'Horses and Divorces', and Billy Strings and Gregory Alan Isakov drop in — sparked by last night's front-to-back album spin.

items.label: 💿 Middle of Nowhere (2026) — Kacey Musgraves
items.note: 🔁 16 plays since May, full spin last night — the album this track is from; her seventh LP and Lost Highway debut, self-produced with Daniel Tashian & Ian Fitchuk.

items.label: Golden Hour (2018) — Kacey Musgraves
items.note: ✨ New to you — the first Musgraves/Tashian/Fitchuk record, the same production trio behind Middle of Nowhere; its graceful country-pop swerve swept all four of its Grammy categories, including Album of the Year.

items.label: Same Trailer Different Park (2013) — Kacey Musgraves
items.note: ✨ New to you — her Grammy-winning major-label debut, produced and co-written with Shane McAnally and Luke Laird: the very same pens behind 'Dry Spell' thirteen years later.

items.label: Blue Umbrella (2020) — Burt Bacharach & Daniel Tashian
items.note: ✨ New to you — co-producer Daniel Tashian's Grammy-nominated songwriting collaboration with a 92-year-old Burt Bacharach: the missing link between Nashville craft and classic pop elegance.

items.label: On The Rocks (2017) — Midland
items.note: ✨ New to you — produced by Shane McAnally and Josh Osborne, two of the 'Dry Spell' co-writers, working the same neo-traditional Texas lane: pedal steel, dancehall shuffle and '70s country gloss.

items.label: Home (2019) — Billy Strings
items.note: ✨ New to you — the bluegrass phenom who guests on 'Everybody Wants To Be A Cowboy'; this breakout LP won the Grammy for Best Bluegrass Album.

items.label: Evening Machines (2018) — Gregory Alan Isakov
items.note: ✨ New to you — the 'Coyote' duet partner's Grammy-nominated folk album: hushed, orchestral late-night songs recorded in a barn studio on his Colorado farm.

items.label: 📻 Kacey Musgraves: Complete Collection (playlist)
items.note: ✨ Her own artist-curated playlist — 132 tracks spanning all seven albums, the catch-all door into the rest of the catalog.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Jimmy Giuffre
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by this morning's "Train and the River" spin — Jimmy Giuffre wrote "Four Brothers" for Woody Herman's big band, then spent his career stripping jazz down to a whisper: this 1957 debut of his drummerless trio with guitarist Jim Hall, "blues-based folk jazz" in his phrase, made "The Train and the River" a minor hit via CBS's The Sound of Jazz special. By 1961 he'd rebuilt the trio with Paul Bley and Steve Swallow and drifted into hushed, chamber-music free improvisation years ahead of Europe's free-improv boom — ignored at the time (the trio folded after a night that paid 35 cents apiece), now cited among the most important groups in jazz history. The quiet lineage runs everywhere: Jim Hall carried the conversational, drummerless idea into Undercurrent with Bill Evans, and ECM later canonized the Bley/Swallow records Fusion and Thesis as "1961".

play_commands.title: Going deeper: Santigold
play_commands.narrative: Dive 2 — past the producer-summit story from the last card and into the buried stuff. Before Santogold existed, Santi White fronted Philly punk band Stiffed alongside future debut-architect John Hill, cutting both their records with Bad Brains bassist Darryl Jenifer — and even earlier she was ghostwriting for Wu-Tang, penning the title track of GZA's Beneath the Surface. Her first-ever credit as 'Santigold' hides on Mark Ronson's Version, and when Diplo & Switch wrapped her debut they immediately built Major Lazer, with her voice on 'Hold the Line.' The one studio album Dive 1 skipped: 2022's Spirituals — Rostam, Boys Noize, Illangelo and SBTRKT — which NPR summed up as 'there's still no one like Santigold.'

play_commands.title: Exploring: Joe Henry
play_commands.narrative: Scar (2001) is where Joe Henry pivoted from alt-country into jazz-noir soul — cut with Marc Ribot, Brad Mehldau, Brian Blade, and Meshell Ndegeocello on bass (the thread that led here from her card), and crowned by an Ornette Coleman alto solo on the opener 'Richard Pryor Addresses a Tearful Nation.' Co-produced with Craig Street, these sessions launched Henry's second career as one of America's great producers — Solomon Burke, Bettye LaVette, and Allen Toussaint records followed, three of them Grammy winners, most cut live in a few days at his Garfield House studio in South Pasadena. One more thread: Scar's 'Stop' was reworked by his sister-in-law Madonna into her hit 'Don't Tell Me.'

play_commands.title: Going deeper: Meshell Ndegeocello
play_commands.narrative: Cards one and two mapped the canon — the producers, the session-player years, the Blue Note run — so dive three heads for the shelves the algorithm skips. There's the Maverick-era closer Comfort Woman and 2007's The World Has Made Me the Man of My Dreams, the sprawl fans keep calling her buried masterpiece (two neighbors from that stretch, Devil's Halo and the Nina Simone tribute Pour une Âme Souveraine, have vanished from Spotify entirely). And the roots and branches get their due: the Chuck Brown and Trouble Funk go-go she apprenticed on as a DC teenager, the Marcus Strickland session she produced, and her drummer Abe Rounds' other life keeping time for Aimee Mann.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Tom Tom Club
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by this morning's Genius of Love spin: when Lee "Scratch" Perry failed to show at Compass Point Studios in 1981, Island boss Chris Blackwell let Talking Heads' rhythm section — Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth — produce their debut themselves with 23-year-old Jamaican engineer Steven Stanley at the desk, while Grace Jones cut Nightclubbing in the studio next door and Sly & Robbie wandered in to clap on "Genius of Love." That track became one of the most sampled recordings in pop history — Grandmaster Flash, Mariah Carey's "Fantasy," 2Pac — and it launched Frantz & Weymouth's second career producing others: Ziggy Marley's Grammy-winning Conscious Party, Happy Mondays' final album, and Shirley Manson's pre-Garbage band Angelfish.

play_commands.title: Going deeper: Meshell Ndegeocello
play_commands.narrative: Card one covered the Comet orbit and her Blue Note production work — this dive goes underneath: before the solo career she was a teenage bassist on DC's go-go circuit with Rare Essence and Little Benny and the Masters, then spent the '90s as everyone's secret-weapon session player (Madonna's Bedtime Stories, the Stones' "Saint of Me", Herbie Hancock's "Nocturnal Sunshine"). The through-lines run both directions: David Gamson of Scritti Politti produced her first two albums and she repaid the favor on 1999's Anomie & Bonhomie, while Bitter producer Craig Street built the same candlelit sound for Cassandra Wilson — who turns up singing on Meshell's own jazz séance, Dance of the Infidel.

Ndegeocello is as much producer as bassist: she helmed Jason Moran's Fats Waller elegy and Marcus Strickland's Nihil Novi for Blue Note, the label where The Omnichord Real Book won the first-ever Best Alternative Jazz Grammy. And the timing is good — Synonym, a duets album with Cynthia Erivo, Cat Power, Chaka Khan and Brandi Carlile, lands October 2, reuniting her with David Gamson, producer of her first two classic albums.

play_commands.title: Exploring: A Certain Ratio
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by this week's Lucinda (EM) plays: 'Lucinda' began life on Sextet (1982) — the first album A Certain Ratio produced themselves after splitting with Factory house producer Martin Hannett ('we thought he was making us sound too much like Joy Division'), its dark funk steeped in the Latin and Cuban percussion of a formative New York stay. The (EM) tag is Andy Meecham (The Emperor Machine), a longtime collaborator who has remixed the original Sextet session tapes for The Joy of Sextet, a 45th-anniversary companion album out 28 August 2026 on Mute alongside Force Majeure, its twin for 1986's Force. ACR were the Factory punk-funk prototype — named after a Brian Eno lyric, signed by Tony Wilson in 1979, openers on Talking Heads' December 1979 UK tour (often credited with nudging David Byrne toward funk) and seedbed for Manchester spin-offs from Swing Out Sister to T-Coy — and they're still evolving on Mute, with Speedy Wunderground's Dan Carey producing 2024's It All Comes Down to This.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Getdown Services
play_commands.narrative: Getdown Services are Ben Sadler and Josh Law — schoolmates from Minehead, Somerset, now Bristol's self-anointed 'Britain's Best Band' — who fuse what Rolling Stone UK calls 'power disco' with unrepentant silliness: seventies/eighties groove music carrying deadpan social commentary. Signed to Bristol indie label Breakfast Records, they came up supporting Fat Dog, Donny Benét and Antony Szmierek, sold out a UK headline tour in 2024, hit Glastonbury in 2025, and play Harry Styles' Meltdown festival this year. 'Cha Cha Slide' — the 'saddest song we've ever written', they told NME — is the third preview of second album Massive Champion, due 14 August via Breakfast Records, a week after this exploration.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Santigold
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by Disparate Youth — a Santigold and Ricky Blaze production with Yeah Yeah Yeahs guitarist Nick Zinner playing that skanking riff. Before she was Santigold, Philadelphia's Santi White fronted the punk band Stiffed and worked the back room, co-writing GZA's 'Beneath the Surface' and producing most of Res's 2001 gem How I Do. Her own records are producer summits: Switch, Diplo and John Hill built the 2008 debut, while Master of My Make-Believe adds Q-Tip, Greg Kurstin, Boys Noize, Buraka Som Sistema and TV on the Radio's Dave Sitek — one reason critics call her a genre of her own. The web runs outward too: vocals for Jay-Z, David Byrne and Tyler, the Creator, and a production turn on Devo's 2010 reunion.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Calvin Harris
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by this week's Garage spin of "Let's Go", this one is about the producer behind the curtain: Calvin Harris (Adam Wiles) recorded his entire debut alone on an Amiga computer in Dumfries, then quietly became pop's most in-demand builder of other people's hits — writing and producing Rihanna's "We Found Love", crafting tracks for Kylie Minogue's X, Dizzee Rascal's Tongue N' Cheek, and The Weeknd's Dawn FM. 18 Months is where the formula crystallized: the DJ as auteur, guests as instruments — BBC Music called it "a collection almost exclusively in the key of triumph," and it made Harris the first artist ever to pull nine UK top-10 singles from one album. The albums below trace both sides: the records he built for others, and the reinventions he kept for himself.

play_commands.title: Exploring: The Polyphonic Spree
play_commands.narrative: Tim DeLaughter answered the 1999 collapse of Tripping Daisy — ended by guitarist Wes Berggren's death — with rock's most improbable rebirth: a two-dozen-strong Dallas collective in white choir robes, chasing the orchestral pop of ELO, the Beach Boys and the 5th Dimension. Their booking demo became the debut "The Beginning Stages of...", and SXSW buzz vaulted them onto David Bowie's 2002 Meltdown festival bill and later his Reality Tour, while "Light & Day" soundtracked Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and became the most-used song in UK advertising. The web runs deep: a pre-fame Annie Clark wore the robes on guitar before becoming St. Vincent, and 2007's The Fragile Army was produced by John Congleton, her future studio partner. (A manual first dig, requested tonight — the Spree is entirely new territory here.)

play_commands.title: Exploring: Frank Zappa
play_commands.narrative: Hot Rats (1969) — the record that sparked this exploration via Peaches En Regalia — was Zappa's first true solo statement, cut just four months after he wrapped production on Captain Beefheart's Trout Mask Replica, trading the Mothers' satire for nearly all-instrumental jazz-rock built with pioneering 16-track overdubbing. The only Mother retained was multi-instrumentalist Ian Underwood (on every track), surrounded by a wild orbit of guests: Beefheart growling the album's lone vocal on Willie the Pimp, French jazz violinist Jean-Luc Ponty, and a teenage Shuggie Otis on bass for Peaches itself. The Guardian's 50th-anniversary piece calls Zappa 'a musical warlock' and credits the album with presaging jazz fusion — the cards below chase that orbit outward through the Beefheart partnership, Ponty's all-Zappa songbook, and the big-band fusion records that extended the Hot Rats idea.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Mikis Theodorakis — beyond the film scores
play_commands.narrative: The Z soundtrack card follows the performers and the film-score world — this one goes into the composer's own catalog, the work that made a military regime consider songs dangerous enough to ban by army decree. In 1960 Theodorakis set Yannis Ritsos's Epitafios with a laïko singer and a bouzouki where polite Athens expected a soprano, detonating the éntekhno revolution — his exact contemporary Manos Hadjidakis (both born 1925) answered with a rival orchestration of the same poems sung by Nana Mouskouri. The great cycles followed: Elytis's Axion Esti as a "popular oratorio," the Mauthausen songs of camp survivor Iakovos Kambanellis that launched his lifelong partnership with Maria Farantouri. Then the junta: Army Decree No. 13 (June 1967) criminalized even listening to his music, and he wrote on through jail, house arrest in Zatouna and the Oropos camp until a campaign led by Shostakovich, Bernstein and Belafonte freed him into Paris exile in April 1970 — Costa-Gavras and Melina Mercouri met his plane. Exile produced the Songs of the Struggle and Neruda's Canto General, sung home to Athens in 1975 after the colonels fell. All of it is new territory in your listening.

items.note: ✨ New to you — The recording that changed Greek music: Ritsos's censored lament sung by laïko star Grigoris Bithikotsis over Manolis Chiotis's bouzouki (1960). Hadjidakis simultaneously issued a rival 'art' version with Nana Mouskouri — the two Epitafios records split Greece. Paired here with Epifania, his Seferis cycle.

items.note: ✨ New to you — His 'popular oratorio' on Odysseas Elytis's epic poem (Elytis won the 1979 Nobel): chorus, orchestra and Bithikotsis's street voice side by side — a landmark of modern Greek culture and many Greeks' pick for the greatest Greek record.

items.note: ✨ New to you — Camp survivor Iakovos Kambanellis wrote the poems; the 1966 cycle premiered the young Maria Farantouri and began their lifelong partnership. Called "the most beautiful musical work ever written about the Holocaust," heard here in the 50th-anniversary performance at the Mauthausen camp itself (May 1995), sung in Greek, Hebrew and English.

Recorded live in Athens in August 1975 — the homecoming year after the junta fell — with Farantouri and Petros Pandis.

items.note: ✨ New to you — The other founder of éntekhno, born the same year (1925): where Theodorakis marched, Hadjidakis dreamed. This instrumental suite is his studio masterpiece — and the rivalry was real: it was Hadjidakis who orchestrated the competing 1960 Epitafios for Nana Mouskouri's voice.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Z (Original Soundtrack) — Mikis Theodorakis
play_commands.narrative: Z (1969) is the rare soundtrack that was itself an act of resistance. When Costa-Gavras filmed his thriller about the assassination of Greek deputy Grigoris Lambrakis, the colonels' junta had banned Theodorakis's music and held the composer in detention — so the score was assembled from music he had already written, used with his blessing rather than composed to picture. Its recurring elegy "To Yelasto Pedi" is his setting of Brendan Behan's "The Laughing Boy" from The Hostage (Greek lyrics by Vasilis Rotas); the main title takes "O Antonis" from his Mauthausen cycle; and "To Palikari Ehi Kaimo" carries the album's one credited voice, Maria Farantouri. The propulsive bouzouki cues made the LP a hit on Columbia and turned Greek laïko into an international sound of defiance. This card follows the performers who realized that music — Farantouri above all — then the Costa-Gavras partnership around the film and its kindred scores (all of it new territory in your listening).

play_commands.title: Exploring: Owen Pallett
play_commands.narrative: Owen Pallett is Toronto's indie orchestrator-in-chief — a violinist-composer who won the first-ever Polaris Prize (as Final Fantasy) and has written string charts for two decades of records, from Arcade Fire's Funeral to Taylor Swift's Red, Pet Shop Boys, and The Last Shadow Puppets. Heartland — sparked by tonight's Midnight Directives play — is the 2010 Domino breakthrough: a baroque-pop concept album where a violent farmer named Lewis addresses his creator, "Owen," over huge looped-violin orchestrations, mixed by Animal Collective producer Rusty Santos. The cards follow the arranger's web outward: Beirut, The Last Shadow Puppets, Grizzly Bear, and the Oscar-nominated Her score with Arcade Fire.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Arash Safaian
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by today's Adagietto play — Tehran-born, Bayreuth-raised composer Arash Safaian wrote This Is (Not) Beethoven (Modern Recordings, 2020) for Beethoven's 250th anniversary: a piano concerto in variation form for Sebastian Knauer and the Zürcher Kammerorchester that treats the canon as living source material. Adagietto slows the famous Allegretto ostinato of the Seventh Symphony into a still, chorale-like meditation — the same Beethoven cell John Corigliano built his 1985 Fantasia on an Ostinato from. It's the second Safaian–Knauer production after 2016's ÜberBach, and sits at the crest of the recomposition wave that runs from Max Richter's Vivaldi to Christian Löffler's shellac reworks.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Thievery Corporation
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by Lebanese Blonde: Thievery Corporation is Rob Garza and Eric Hilton, who started mixing dub, bossa nova and Indian classical records above their own Eighteenth Street Lounge in DC in 1995 — then built the ESL label around the sound. The Mirror Conspiracy (2000) is that bar distilled into 'loungetronic' espionage-cool (Tinnitist), with jazz vocalist Pam Bricker carrying Lebanese Blonde all the way to the Garden State soundtrack. Their world radiates outward through ESL: Hilton produced Federico Aubele's Gran Hotel Buenos Aires and DC reggae band The Archives, early Thievery cuts rode Kruder & Dorfmeister's 1996 DJ-Kicks across Europe, and later albums drafted David Byrne, Perry Farrell and Emilíana Torrini.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Kangding Ray
play_commands.narrative: Kangding Ray is David Letellier — a French architect turned Berlin electronic auteur whose score for Óliver Laxe's desert-rave odyssey Sirāt won the Cannes Soundtrack Award and carried the film to two Academy Award nominations. Before landing on Invada he spent a decade on Carsten Nicolai and Olaf Bender's raster-noton label, building techno with an architect's precision — club music that always behaved like score. Start with Sirāt, then trace the lineage back through the granite minimalism of Solens Arc to the guitar-flecked glitch of his early records. Entirely uncharted territory: not a single Kangding Ray play in your history.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Phineas Newborn Jr.
play_commands.narrative: Phineas Newborn Jr. is jazz piano's great tragic virtuoso: a Memphis prodigy whose family band was the Plantation Inn house band, backed B.B. King's first 1949 recordings, and played on the 'Rocket 88' session — and whose signature blistering lines improvised in parallel octaves, both hands in unison, led Oscar Peterson to call him the best all-around pianist to follow him and Leonard Feather to rank him among the three greatest of all time. Yet critics kept branding the brilliance 'too technical,' and the wound went deep: breakdowns, stays at Camarillo State Hospital, a hand injury, and a fade into underrecorded obscurity so stark that his plight helped spur the founding of the Jazz Foundation of America. His core legacy is exactly what you asked for — 50s/60s trio and quartet dates, from the Atlantic debut through the one-off We Three summit to the L.A. Contemporary run — and every one of them is new to you.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Sonny Rollins
play_commands.narrative: Sonny Rollins — who died this past May at 95 — came up through the Clifford Brown–Max Roach quintet and a stint with Miles Davis, then spent 1956–62 as hard bop's most rigorous small-group thinker, pioneering the pianoless tenor-bass-drums trio ("strolling") that Joe Henderson, Branford Marsalis, and Joshua Redman all borrowed. He was also jazz's great self-critic: at the height of his fame in 1959 he quit performing for two years to practice up to 15 hours a day on the Williamsburg Bridge walkway, returning in 1962 with a Jim Hall quartet on The Bridge. You've never played a Rollins-led date, so this card maps exactly what you asked for — his 50s/60s trios and quartets, every one new to you.

play_commands.title: Exploring: The Modern Jazz Quartet
play_commands.narrative: The Modern Jazz Quartet grew straight out of Dizzy Gillespie's late-'40s big band — pianist John Lewis, vibraphonist Milt Jackson, and bebop drum pioneer Kenny Clarke were its rhythm section before incorporating as a cooperative with bassist Percy Heath in 1952 (Connie Kay took the drum chair in 1955 and held it for four decades). Under Lewis's direction they invented a niche of their own: tuxedoed concert-hall jazz built on baroque fugues and counterpoint yet anchored by Jackson's blues-drenched vibes — the tension between those two voices IS the MJQ sound. Signed to Atlantic by Nesuhi Ertegun in 1956, they became the flagship of 'third stream' music, collaborating with Sonny Rollins, Jimmy Giuffre, Laurindo Almeida, and the Swingle Singers. Completely new to your library — six doors in below.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Wooden Elephant
play_commands.narrative: Wooden Elephant are a contemporary-classical string quintet who play entire electronic albums acoustically, formed in 2017 at Germany's PODIUM Esslingen festival around Irish violist-arranger Ian Anderson — who caught the bug touring with Jonny Greenwood and the London Contemporary Orchestra and playing on Radiohead's A Moon Shaped Pool. Their Radiohead-sanctioned Kid A recycling (Backlash Music, 2021) put knives, glue and bowed everyday objects on record and landed two tracks in AppleTV+'s Swan Song; since then they've recorded Moor Mother's Analog Fluids of Sonic Black Holes with the Beethoven Orchestra Bonn, turned SOPHIE into a ballet, and staged Aphex Twin's Drukqs with prepared piano — next up, a Verbier-commissioned rework of Miles Davis's In a Silent Way for his 2026 centenary. First Wooden Elephant entry in your log, though you've been circling their repertoire all year: Drukqs, Homogenic and Radiohead are already in rotation.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Fretwork
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by this morning's Qobuz run through the Fantazias. In the summer of 1680 the 21-year-old Purcell filled a manuscript with fantazias for viols — deliberately archaic music, written after the violin had already displaced the viol at court, and the last great flowering of a two-century English consort tradition running from Byrd and Gibbons through Lawes, Jenkins and his mentor Matthew Locke. Their harmonic audacity still startles: Savall's label ranks the set with Bach's Art of Fugue as a "sum" of polyphonic thinking. Fretwork has recorded the cycle twice — Gramophone calls their reading "the classic" — and this 2009 harmonia mundi album is the ensemble's second traversal.

items.note: ✨ New to you — Gramophone: 'explores the innermost reaches of this repertory'. Savall's darker, more meditative viol sound is the classic counterweight to Fretwork's clarity.

items.text: The viol consort was already antique when Purcell wrote these — Charles II preferred French violins — making the fantazias a private farewell to a 200-year English tradition. The composers below are that tradition: Purcell's mentor Matthew Locke (whose death in 1677 he mourned in an elegy), and the Caroline masters Lawes and Jenkins.

items.label: Matthew Locke: The Flat Consort (2022) — Fretwork
items.note: ✨ New to you — Purcell's mentor at court; quicksilver, harmonically strange suites that point straight at the fantazias.

items.label: Lawes: Consorts in Six Parts (2003) — Phantasm
items.note: ✨ New to you — the wildest harmonic imagination of the pre-Civil War court; Lawes was killed at the siege of Chester in 1645.

items.label: John Jenkins: Complete Four-Part Consort Music (2018) — Fretwork
items.note: ✨ New to you — the gentle giant of the mid-century consort, with some 800 works to his name; the bridge between Byrd’s generation and Purcell’s.

items.label: Chaconnes and Fantasias: Music of Britten and Purcell (2017) — Emerson String Quartet
items.note: ✨ New to you — pairs these fantasias with Britten, whose String Quartet No. 2 (written 1945 for Purcell's 250th anniversary) ends in a monumental Chacony in homage.

items.label: If: Michael Nyman, Henry Purcell (2019) — Iestyn Davies & Fretwork
items.note: ✨ New to you — Nyman built his early style on Purcell grounds (The Draughtsman’s Contract); here Fretwork themselves interleave Nyman songs with the Purcell that inspired them.

items.note: ✨ New to you — variations and fugue on a Purcell theme (from Abdelazer): the 20th century's most famous Purcell homage, in Britten's own Decca recording.

items.text: Founded in 1986 and still the world’s leading viol consort, Fretwork has spent four decades proving the instrument isn’t a museum piece — from Byrd and Dowland to Bach arrangements and new music (one early collection appeared only in Japan, on Ryuichi Sakamoto’s label).

play_commands.title: Exploring: The Joubert Singers
play_commands.narrative: In 1982, Phyliss McKoy Joubert — Minister of Music at the First Baptist Church in Crown Heights — recorded “Stand on the Word” with a children's choir for a privately pressed gospel LP, Somebody Prayed For This, and Brooklyn's DJs turned it into one of dance music's great crossover stories. Tony Humphries broke it at New Jersey's Zanzibar and cut the official 1985 remix for Next Plateau, while the collector-bait “Larry Levan remix” is pure myth — Red Bull Music Academy traced it to a 2003 bootleg white label; no such mix ever existed. Walter Gibbons, disco's first remix visionary, lived down the block from the church and championed the original pressing, and the song's echo runs from Paradise Garage lore to Justice's “D.A.N.C.E.” Sparked by today's play of the 1982 version — here's the gospel-to-dancefloor web around it.

suggestions.genre_source: web search snippets: Wikipedia 'funk, post-disco, soul'; NTS 'gospel, funk and soul group led by Phyliss McKoy Joubert'

play_commands.title: Exploring: Hermanos Gutiérrez
play_commands.narrative: Alejandro and Estevan Gutiérrez began recording two-guitar instrumentals in Zürich in 2015, channeling their Ecuadorian mother's homeland through 1950s Latin America and Morricone's deserts — 'music that sings without needing a singer.' Then Dan Auerbach of The Black Keys signed them to Easy Eye Sound: he has produced their last three records in Nashville (earning a Producer of the Year Grammy in part for that work) and steered them into their first vocal track with Leon Bridges, while the brothers repaid the Latin songbook by guesting on Natalia Lafourcade's Latin Grammy-winning Cancionera. A fitting close to this international run — the trail below leads from Easy Eye's studio family back to the Cuban-American guitar-duo records this sound descends from.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Anouar Brahem
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by December's immersion in After the Last Sky — Tunisian oud master Anouar Brahem has spent 35 years turning the oud into a chamber-music voice on ECM, every album produced by label founder Manfred Eicher since 1991's Barzakh. His discography is a map of partnerships: Dave Holland has been his anchor since 1998's Thimar with John Surman, expanding into the Blue Maqams quartet with Jack DeJohnette and Django Bates, while a parallel French trio with pianist François Couturier and accordionist Jean-Louis Matinier carries his impressionist side. He sums up his signature in two words — 'maqam blues': Arab modal tradition crossed with jazz and the elegiac impressionism of early-20th-century French music.

play_commands.title: Exploring: BALTHVS
play_commands.narrative: BALTHVS is the Bogotá trio of Balthazar Aguirre (guitar), Johanna Mercuriana (bass) and Santiago Lizcano (drums), and everything runs in-house: Aguirre produces the records himself (Harvest was mixed with Lizcano in La Mesa, Colombia), they release independently, and in six years they've stacked four LPs, twelve EPs and 100M+ streams. Their blend of psychedelic funk, cumbia, surf and Middle Eastern melody made them a pillar of the global chill-psych wave alongside Khruangbin, Glass Beams and Hermanos Gutiérrez — the kick that sparked this exploration. 2026's Transmutations 'alchemizes' their live show into studio form, and a brand-new album, Manifest, lands this October.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Orquesta Akokán
play_commands.narrative: Orquesta Akokán began as a three-way collaboration between NYC producer Jacob Plasse, arranger Mike Eckroth, and Cuban vocalist José "Pepito" Gómez, who flew to Havana and — with help from Irakere's César López — assembled an all-star banda gigante to cut Daptone's first-ever Spanish-language release live to tape in three days at the storied Estudios Areito. The Grammy-nominated 2018 debut deliberately channels the golden-era mambo of Pérez Prado, Beny Moré, and Machito, and the band has kept that engine running through 16 Rayos (2021), Caracoles (2024), and this year's América!, tracked live to tape by Daptone co-founder Gabriel Roth. Plasse's other band, Los Hacheros, works the same vintage-Cuba vein from Brooklyn in a stripped-down charanga format. (Explored from chat mid-international-music kick, sparked by an Ibibio Sound Machine session.)

play_commands.title: Exploring: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan
play_commands.narrative: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan — Shahenshah-e-Qawwali, the "king of kings" of the six-century-old Sufi devotional tradition — was carried to the West by Peter Gabriel's Real World label after his 1985 WOMAD appearance, and his two Michael Brook–produced albums there, Mustt Mustt (1990) and the Grammy-nominated Night Song (1996), remain the great bridges between qawwali and Western studios. His orbit is remarkable: Massive Attack's remix of "Mustt Mustt" put qawwali on UK dance floors, Eddie Vedder duetted with him on the Dead Man Walking soundtrack, his voice appears on scores for Scorsese, Stone and Tim Robbins films, and Jeff Buckley called him "my Elvis." This exploration was sparked from chat mid-session of gospel choirs and Ibibio Sound Machine — the ecstatic-devotional-voice kinship runs straight through qawwali.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Ezra Collective
play_commands.narrative: Sparked by today's Ibibio Sound Machine session: Ezra Collective are the London quintet who took UK jazz from Gary Crosby's Tomorrow's Warriors youth programme to the 2023 Mercury Prize and, in 2025, the first-ever jazz Brit Award for Group of the Year. Led by drummer Femi Koleoso — who also holds down the drum chair for Gorillaz — with keyboardist Joe Armon-Jones, they self-produce with engineer Riccardo Damian (mixes by Eric Lau), folding Fela Kuti's Afrobeat, dub, salsa and grime into big-hearted dancefloor jazz. Their guest lists read like a map of the London scene — Jorja Smith, Loyle Carner, Sampa the Great, Kojey Radical, Nao, Yazmin Lacey — and a fourth album, Here Because of Hope, arrives September 18 on Partisan with Pa Salieu, Lila Iké and Letitia Wright.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Damon Albarn
play_commands.narrative: Your first Damon Albarn solo play — 'Mr Tembo', his ukulele ode to a Tanzanian baby elephant (sung with the Leytonstone City Mission Choir), filled the whole house yesterday morning. The thread to pull is producer Richard Russell of XL Recordings: he produced Everyday Robots, made Gil Scott-Heron's I'm New Here (you've played Gil 12 times since October), and co-produced Bobby Womack's The Bravest Man in the Universe WITH Albarn — you played its title track just last month. Beyond the Russell axis, Albarn's collaboration web runs from his supergroup with The Clash's Paul Simonon and Afrobeat drummer Tony Allen to producing Amadou & Mariam's Welcome to Mali — and you already know his day job: 12 Gorillaz plays in your history.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Brian Eno
play_commands.narrative: You've logged 62 Brian Eno plays since Aug 2025 — almost all on the ambient side: Apollo (19 plays, most recently Deep Blue Day in the Basement Study) and Music for Airports (17), with Harold Budd as your #1 session neighbor (59 co-plays). But Eno's other life is the producer's chair: three straight Talking Heads albums, Devo's debut, U2's Achtung Baby, Bowie's Outside — plus collaborator credits with Fripp, Byrne and John Cale. This card leans into that lineage: the Byrne sampling landmark you've never played, the Talking Heads masterpiece you've only touched once, and the Fripp & Eno loops you've been circling all spring.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Spare solo classical — after Yo-Yo Ma's Bach & Gould
play_commands.artist: Pablo Casals, Hilary Hahn, Víkingur Ólafsson, Arvo Pärt, Keith Jarrett
play_commands.narrative: You told me you love the spare, meditative quality of Yo-Yo Ma's Bach cello suites and Glenn Gould's solo repertoire — one instrument, one voice, no ornament. These five records live in that same quiet room: the historic recordings Ma descends from, the solo-violin and solo-piano siblings of that repertoire, and two meditations from outside the baroque — Pärt's near-silence and Jarrett's improvised cathedral.

items.label: 💿 Hilary Hahn plays Bach (1997) — Hilary Hahn
items.note: The solo-violin sibling of the cello suites — Bach's Sonatas & Partitas, recorded at 17 with astonishing stillness and clarity.

items.label: 💿 Johann Sebastian Bach (2018) — Víkingur Ólafsson
items.note: Widely called Gould's heir — crystalline, spare solo-piano Bach; if you love the Goldbergs, this is the modern room next door.

items.note: Perhaps the most meditative record ECM ever made — Für Alina and Spiegel im Spiegel, music built from silence; the spare aesthetic taken to its limit.

items.note: Solo piano meditation from the improvised side of the aisle — the best-selling solo piano album ever, one man alone filling a dark opera house.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Elis Regina
play_commands.narrative: Tonight you played seven tracks from Elis & Tom straight through the whole house — your first Elis Regina session on record. The 1974 album was cut at MGM Studios in Los Angeles to mark her tenth anniversary with Philips, produced by Aloysio de Oliveira — Jobim's longtime Elenco-label producer — with Elis's pianist-husband César Camargo Mariano doubling Jobim's keyboards alongside Hélio Delmiro, Oscar Castro-Neves and Luizão Maia. Mariano is the thread through her whole golden run (Elis '72, Falso Brilhante), and before Jobim she made her name championing then-unknown songwriters Gilberto Gil, Milton Nascimento and Chico Buarque, plus jazz collaborations with Toots Thielemans and Hermeto Pascoal.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Jimmie Noone
play_commands.narrative: First time exploring Jimmie Noone — 'Chicago Rhythm' just introduced you to one of the 'big three' New Orleans clarinetists of the 1920s, alongside Johnny Dodds and Sidney Bechet (who, at age 13, was actually Noone's clarinet teacher). His 1928 Apex Club Orchestra sides — cut with Earl Hines moonlighting from the Louis Armstrong Hot Five sessions — are the smooth, swinging counterpoint to Dodds' and Bechet's cutting styles, and the teenage Benny Goodman stood in that Chicago club studying him; Maurice Ravel even said Boléro was partly based on a Noone improvisation. He kept leading Chicago bands until 1944, when he died mid-comeback while playing weekly on Orson Welles' radio show with Kid Ory's all-star New Orleans band. (Source: Syncopated Times 'Profiles in Jazz' by Scott Yanow.)

play_commands.title: Exploring: Chico Buarque
play_commands.narrative: Three albums from Andrew's Apple Music library trace Chico Buarque's arc from festival-era songwriter to protest-era master of MPB. Vol. 3 (1968) captures the stretch just before censorship pressure drove him into Italian exile; Nº 4 (1970) is the record he cut on his return to a hardened dictatorship; and Construção (1971) is the masterpiece that followed, its title track a samba that narrates a construction worker's death in strict proparoxytone verse. All three sit at the heart of MPB's golden run.

play_commands.title: Exploring: 60s Trombone in Small Groups
play_commands.narrative: You asked for 60s jazz trombonists working in small settings — this card runs the full spectrum: the two-bone summit of J.J. Johnson and Kai Winding with Bill Evans comping, Curtis Fuller's warm Savoy-era quintet, Grachan Moncur III's inside-outside Blue Note dates with Lee Morgan and a teenage Tony Williams, Bob Brookmeyer's valve trombone alongside Stan Getz and Herbie Hancock, Julian Priester a decade before Mwandishi, and Roswell Rudd out at the free frontier with the New York Art Quartet. Trios were rare for trombone in the 60s — quartets and quintets are where the instrument breathed.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Bach Trios
play_commands.artist: Yo-Yo Ma, Chris Thile & Edgar Meyer
play_commands.narrative: Bach Trios (2017, Nonesuch) — cut in James Taylor's barn studio in western Massachusetts — is mostly keyboard Bach reborn as a three-way string conversation: Well-Tempered Clavier preludes and fugues, chorale preludes, an organ trio sonata and the G-minor gamba sonata, with Thile's mandolin deputizing for the harpsichord (PopMatters, 9/10 — the first record these three ever made as a bare trio). The Yo-Yo Ma card from earlier today already covers the gamba-sonata discography and the trio's own orbit (Goat Rodeo, Appalachia Waltz, Thile's solo Bach) — this card follows the album's real subject: what happens when a small group takes Bach's counterpoint into its own hands. Two main paths below: consorts and trios playing the same repertoire straight, and sixty-plus years of jazz musicians treating Bach as raw material.

suggestions.genre_source: PopMatters review tags: baroque, classical; 2017 Nonesuch album of Bach arrangements for cello, mandolin & double bass

items.label: 💿 Bach Trios (2017) — Yo-Yo Ma, Chris Thile & Edgar Meyer
items.note: The album that started this exploration

items.text: Bach's organ trio sonatas were written as three fully independent voices — two manuals and pedals — which is exactly why they survive transplanting to any three instruments. That makes Bach Trios less a novelty than the newest entry in a very old tradition: small groups re-scoring Bach's counterpoint for whatever hands are in the room.

items.label: Bach: Trio Sonatas, BWV 525–530 (2002) — London Baroque
items.note: The six organ trio sonatas — the same wellspring Bach Trios draws its Trio Sonata No. 6 from — re-scored for two violins and continuo.

items.label: Bach: Organ Trio Sonatas, BWV 525–530 (2012) — Florilegium
items.note: Period-instrument chamber re-scorings of the organ trio sonatas — flute, violin and continuo, one-per-part (Channel Classics). Stands in for Rachel Podger & Brecon Baroque's 2017 set, which isn't on Spotify.

items.label: J.S. Bach: The Art of Fugue (2002) — Fretwork
items.note: Bach's final fugue cycle was printed in open score with no instrumentation specified — Fretwork's viols make the case that it is really consort music.

items.label: Bach: The Well-Tempered Consort I (2020) — Phantasm
items.note: Laurence Dreyfus's viol consort turns Well-Tempered Clavier preludes and fugues into consort polyphony — the same WTC pool Bach Trios raids.

items.label: Play Bach No. 1 (1959) — Jacques Loussier Trio
items.note: The record that invented the jazz-Bach franchise — piano-trio swing on preludes and toccatas that sold millions of copies and ran to five volumes.

items.label: Jazz Sébastien Bach (1963) — The Swingle Singers
items.note: Scat-sung Bach over bass and brushes — released in the US as Bach's Greatest Hits, it won the group the 1964 Best New Artist Grammy.

items.note: A Nonesuch labelmate's answer a year after Bach Trios: WTC preludes and fugues, each followed by a new Mehldau piece composed 'after' it.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Yo-Yo Ma, Chris Thile & Edgar Meyer
play_commands.album: J.S. Bach: Sonata for Viola da Gamba No. 3 in G Minor, BWV 1029
play_commands.narrative: First logged play of Yo-Yo Ma — arrived via Sonos/Qobuz with Bach Trios, the 2017 Nonesuch album that recasts Bach for mandolin, cello, and double bass, recorded with Chris Thile and Edgar Meyer in James Taylor's barn studio. The source work, the Gamba Sonata No. 3 in G minor BWV 1029, is the most concerto-like of Bach's three gamba sonatas — its driving Vivace so orchestral that scholars have dubbed it 'a seventh Brandenburg,' and Anner Bylsma suspected it began as a lost concerto. This arrangement is the latest chapter in a 40-year recorded history that runs from Savall's 1977 reference recording to Boulanger's 2011 benchmark — and in Ma and Meyer's own crossover lineage going back to 1996's Appalachia Waltz.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Nils Petter Molvær
play_commands.narrative: Your first exploration of Nils Petter Molvær — you've been working through Be Quiet (2026), his new Edition Records album built as nine duo encounters recorded in nine cities (Amsterdam is one of them; alva noto and Imogen Heap are among the partners). Molvær is the pioneer of Norwegian future jazz: his 1997 ECM debut Khmer fused processed trumpet with electronic soundscapes and hip-hop beats, breaking the ECM chamber-jazz mold so hard the label released its first-ever singles from it. His collaboration web runs deep — career-long guitarist Eivind Aarset, dub legends Sly & Robbie (Nordub), dub-techno inventor Moritz von Oswald (1/1), and Bill Laswell's Tabla Beat Science.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Catherine Ribeiro + Alpes
play_commands.narrative: Your first brush with Catherine Ribeiro + Alpes — one play of 'Paix' last night. Alpes was the French-Portuguese singer's psychedelic avant-folk vehicle, built around multi-instrumentalist Patrice Moullet and his invented instruments (the buzzsaw-like 'cosmophone'), and Paix (1972) is widely considered her masterpiece — with Patrice Lemoine of space-rockers Gong driving its relentless organ. Ribeiro started out acting in Godard's Les Carabiniers and translating Dylan into French; decades later Kim Gordon and Jim O'Rourke became her most vocal champions, and the albums were unavailable in the US until Anthology Recordings' 2018 reissues (Pitchfork).

play_commands.title: Exploring: Sierra Ferrell
play_commands.narrative: Sierra Ferrell is a West Virginia-born singer-songwriter who went from freight-hopping busker to four-time Grammy winner with her 2024 album Trail of Flowers. Both her major-label albums were produced by Gary Paczosa, the Nashville veteran behind Alison Krauss and Dolly Parton records — that shared production lineage connects her to the deepest roots of bluegrass and Americana. Her collaboration web is remarkable: she's guested with Zach Bryan ('Holy Roller,' #37 Hot 100), The Black Keys (backing vocals on Dropout Boogie), Shakey Graves, Ray LaMontagne, Post Malone, Mumford & Sons (SNL 2026), and most recently Beck. Her sound blends folk, bluegrass, gypsy jazz, tango, and country in a way that's genuinely genre-defying — start with Trail of Flowers for the polished vision, then go back to Long Time Coming for the raw magic.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Archie Bell & the Drells
play_commands.narrative: Archie Bell & the Drells were a Houston R&B vocal group who topped both the pop and R&B charts in 1968 with 'Tighten Up,' a funky dance jam backed by the T.S.U. Toronadoes that put Texas soul on the national map. What makes them fascinating is the production lineage: they were one of the earliest acts produced by Kenneth Gamble & Leon Huff before the duo founded Philadelphia International Records, making the Drells a direct link between Southern soul and the Philly Sound that shaped disco. Their later albums on Philadelphia International featured MFSB's house band — the same musicians behind The O'Jays, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, and Billy Paul — and Thom Bell also co-produced several of their singles.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Massive Attack
play_commands.narrative: Massive Attack are the architects of trip-hop, emerging from Bristol's Wild Bunch sound system in 1988. Their production lineage is remarkably deep: Blue Lines (1991) was co-produced by Jonny Dollar and executive-produced by Cameron McVey (Neneh Cherry's partner), Protection (1994) brought in Nellee Hooper (also ex-Wild Bunch, later produced Björk's Debut), and from Mezzanine (1998) onward, Neil Davidge became their key co-producer. Their collaboration web is extraordinary — Elizabeth Fraser (Cocteau Twins) sang Teardrop, Tracey Thorn (Everything but the Girl) voiced the Protection title track, founding member Tricky left to make Maxinquaye, and Horace Andy has been their spiritual voice across every album. Recent work includes a 2026 collaboration with Tom Waits on 'Boots on the Ground' and 2016 EPs featuring Young Fathers, Roots Manuva, and Hope Sandoval.

play_commands.title: Exploring: DJ Shadow
play_commands.narrative: DJ Shadow (Joshua Paul Davis) is one of the most influential figures in instrumental hip hop — his 1996 debut Endtroducing..... holds the Guinness World Record as the first album made entirely from samples, produced on an AKAI MPC60 II with help from Dan the Automator's Pro Tools rig. His collaboration web is extraordinary: he produced UNKLE's Psyence Fiction (1998) featuring Thom Yorke, Richard Ashcroft, and Mike D; co-founded the Solesides label with Blackalicious and Lyrics Born; partnered with Cut Chemist on the legendary Brainfreeze and Product Placement mixtapes; and has worked with Run the Jewels, Nas, Ghostface Killah, De La Soul, Raekwon, Zack de la Rocha, DJ Krush, and Massive Attack. His recent double album Our Pathetic Age (2019) bridges his instrumental mastery with a who's-who of hip hop collaborators.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Fleetwood Mac
play_commands.narrative: Dreams is one of the crown jewels of Rumours, Fleetwood Mac's 1977 masterpiece self-produced with engineers Ken Caillat and Richard Dashut — a production partnership that also shaped Tango in the Night a decade later. The band's story is a web of collaborations: Stevie Nicks and Lindsey Buckingham were a folk-rock duo before Mick Fleetwood recruited them, Peter Green founded the band as a British blues outfit after leaving John Mayall's Bluesbreakers (where he'd replaced Eric Clapton), and Christine McVie came from Chicken Shack. Each member's solo work — Nicks' Bella Donna with Tom Petty, Buckingham's meticulous solo albums — carries Fleetwood Mac DNA, and the band's later incarnation brought in Neil Finn of Crowded House and Mike Campbell of the Heartbreakers.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Milton Nascimento
play_commands.narrative: Milton Nascimento is the voice of Minas Gerais — the founder of the Clube da Esquina movement that fused Brazilian folk, jazz, rock, and choral harmonies into something utterly unique. Clube Da Esquina (1972), co-credited with Lô Borges, was produced by Milton Miranda and featured a collective including Toninho Horta, Beto Guedes, and Wagner Tiso. His international breakthrough came through Wayne Shorter's Native Dancer (1974), which led to collaborations with Herbie Hancock, Pat Metheny, Paul Simon, Peter Gabriel, and Esperanza Spalding — an extraordinary web of connections spanning MPB, jazz, and art rock.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Khaled
play_commands.narrative: First time exploring Khaled — the King of Raï, born in Oran, Algeria. "Didi" was a monster 1992 hit produced by Don Was (Rolling Stones, Bob Dylan, Bonnie Raitt), who assembled Was (Not Was) band members and played bass himself, blending Linn 9000 loops with live Algerian percussion. The other half of the self-titled album was produced by Michael Brook, known for his work with Youssou N'Dour and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan — a direct bridge from raï to the wider world music landscape. Khaled's later albums brought in Philippe Eidel (arranger of Balkan, Peter Brook's Mahabharata), Clive Hunt (reggae producer), and even French chansonnier Jean-Jacques Goldman, making Sahra (1996) a genre-defying masterpiece praised as 'celestial brilliance' by Time Out.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Bill Evans
play_commands.narrative: You've been deep in the Complete Bill Evans On Verve box set via Apple Music in the Media Room — 13 tracks in one session covering the McFarland orchestral collaborations through the solo trio cuts. That JazzTimes review nails it: the box's real treasure is the unissued Philly Joe Jones/Eddie Gomez Village Vanguard sessions from 1967 and the Larry Bunker/Chuck Israels Trident Club dates. Your session neighbors tell the story — McCoy Tyner, Herbie Hancock, Monk, Oscar Peterson — you're swimming in the deep end of piano jazz. Evans' collaboration web is extraordinary: he was Miles Davis's pianist on Kind of Blue (1959), recorded the intimate guitar-piano masterpiece Undercurrent with Jim Hall (1962), made two sublime duo albums with Tony Bennett (1975-76), and the Verve set captures his chamber music sessions with Gary McFarland and his explosive Stan Getz date with Elvin Jones on drums.

play_commands.title: Exploring: The Delfonics
play_commands.narrative: The Delfonics are the seed crystal of the Philadelphia Sound — William "Poogie" Hart's falsetto paired with producer Thom Bell's lush string arrangements created the blueprint that every sweet soul group from the Stylistics to the Spinners would follow. Bell co-wrote nearly every Delfonics hit with Hart and invented a production style that sandpapered away Southern soul's grit, replacing the backbeat with swirling orchestration. This is your first listen — and Tarantino thought enough of "Didn't I" to build an entire romance around it in Jackie Brown. The Thom Bell production tree is deep: from Dusty Springfield's Philly sessions to the Spinners' Atlantic run to his 2025 Rock Hall induction.

play_commands.album: The Best Of Decca Years Volume 2: The Composer
play_commands.narrative: Your 'Swing That Music' play is a deep cut — Ricky Riccardi, the 21st century's foremost Armstrong authority, named it one of his five 'painful cuts' just outside the 20 Essential Armstrong Recordings. The 1936 single came from the Decca period when Armstrong, managed by Joe Glaser, fronted Luis Russell's big band and became a box-office sensation breaking Benny Goodman's Paramount Theater record. Armstrong's collaboration web spans the entire first century of recorded music: he recorded with King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band in 1923, dueled Sidney Bechet on 'Cake Walking Babies' in 1925, invented the soloist's art with Earl Hines on 'West End Blues' in 1928, was first paired with Ella Fitzgerald by producer Milt Gabler at Decca in 1949, and recorded with Duke Ellington in 1961 when Ellington surprised him in the studio with 'Azalea' — a tune Duke had written decades earlier with Armstrong specifically in mind.

play_commands.title: Exploring: M. Ward
play_commands.narrative: M. Ward is a Portland analog purist who still demos every song on the same 4-track cassette recorder he's had since he was fifteen — a devotion to lo-fi warmth that comes directly from his hero John Fahey, whose Transfiguration of Blind Joe Death inspired this album's title. The track you heard is his Bowie cover of Let's Dance, featured in the 2007 film Eagle vs Shark. Ward's real superpower is the collaboration web: he produced all six She & Him albums with Zooey Deschanel, co-produced Jenny Lewis's debut Rabbit Fur Coat, produced records for Mavis Staples and Valerie June, and formed the supergroup Monsters of Folk with Jim James (My Morning Jacket), Conor Oberst, and Mike Mogis (Bright Eyes). He's played on Norah Jones's Not Too Late, toured as her guitarist, performed on records by Cat Power, Neko Case, Brian Wilson, Beth Orton, and Kim Deal. His Post-War album featured Jim James and Neko Case; Hold Time brought in Jason Lytle of Grandaddy and Lucinda Williams; More Rain added Peter Buck (R.E.M.) and k.d. lang.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Marvin Gaye
play_commands.narrative: Marvin Gaye self-produced Let's Get It On with co-writer Ed Townsend at Hitsville and Motown's LA studios — a record AllMusic calls 'unparalleled in its sheer sensuality,' the blueprint for every slow jam that followed. His arc from Smokey Robinson-produced early Motown hits through the socially conscious What's Going On to the erotic minimalism of this album is one of the great artistic evolutions in American music. The Leon Ware connection is the hidden gem: Ware wrote and produced the entire I Want You album (1976), songs he'd originally intended for his own Musical Massage LP — Gaye heard the demos and claimed them.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Beck
play_commands.narrative: Beck Hansen is a one-man genre demolition crew from East LA — a folk-punk kid who taught himself to sample by rewiring thrift-store turntables, then spent three decades shapeshifting through every producer relationship in indie rock. Colors is his sugar-rush pop album with Greg Kurstin (Adele, Foo Fighters), but the real story is the producer lineage: the Dust Brothers turned him into a sample-collage genius on Odelay, Nigel Godrich (Radiohead's longtime producer) gave him orchestral grandeur on Sea Change and Morning Phase (which beat Beyoncé for Album of the Year), and Danger Mouse pulled him into psychedelic minimalism on Modern Guilt. He's also a prolific producer himself — he made Charlotte Gainsbourg's IRM and Thurston Moore's Demolished Thoughts. In your library he's been playing across the whole Cap Hill house alongside Nina Simone and Thundercat sessions.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Thundercat
play_commands.narrative: Thundercat (Stephen Lee Bruner) is one of the most interconnected musicians in modern LA — a funk-jazz-soul virtuoso bassist from Compton who started in Suicidal Tendencies at 16 before Flying Lotus pulled him into the Brainfeeder orbit. His bass lines form the backbone of Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly (winning a Grammy for "These Walls"), and he's a founding member of the West Coast Get Down collective with childhood friend Kamasi Washington. Drunk is his sprawling 23-track third album — mixing funk, psychedelia, acid jazz, and absurdist humor with features from Kenny Loggins to Pharrell.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Glenn Gould
play_commands.narrative: Glenn Gould's 1956 recording of Beethoven's last three piano sonatas was his second album for Columbia, following the Goldberg Variations that had made him famous overnight. Where critics celebrated the Goldbergs, this 'feisty and headstrong' treatment of Beethoven's pianistic 'New Testament' outraged them — Gould approached these transcendent late works with contrapuntal clarity and rhythmic drive, refusing the weighty, reverential tradition of Schnabel and Kempff. These three sonatas, composed 1820–1822, represent Beethoven's final statement in the form, culminating in Op. 111's otherworldly Arietta variations.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Keith Mansfield
play_commands.narrative: You've played Funky Fanfare 4 times — that iconic brass riff is Keith Mansfield's signature, originally composed for the KPM 1000 library music series in the late 1960s and later made famous by NFL Films and Quentin Tarantino's Death Proof. Mansfield wasn't just a library composer — he arranged for Dusty Springfield's 'Dusty... Definitely' (1968), orchestrated Love Affair's 'Everlasting Love,' and produced Maynard Ferguson's M.F. Horn albums, connecting him to the jazz-funk world. He was also a member of The Mohawks and a core contributor to the KPM 1000 Series alongside Alan Hawkshaw — their work has been sampled by Danger Mouse, Madlib, Fatboy Slim, and Denzel Curry, making this unassuming library music catalog one of the most pillaged sample sources in hip-hop history.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Harry Nilsson
play_commands.narrative: Harry Nilsson was the reclusive genius of early-'70s pop — never toured, never performed live, yet both Lennon and McCartney named him their favorite American artist. Nilsson Schmilsson was produced by Richard Perry at Trident Studios in London with session heavyweights like Jim Gordon (Derek and the Dominos) on drums and Herbie Flowers on bass — the same Richard Perry who produced Carly Simon's 'You're So Vain' and Barbra Streisand's Stoney End. The Nilsson rabbit hole runs deep: a whole album of Randy Newman covers, a John Lennon-produced lost weekend record, and he's the reason Aerosmith got their name (from his album Aerial Ballet).

play_commands.title: Exploring: Daft Punk
play_commands.narrative: You've played 34 Daft Punk tracks in your library — Lose Yourself to Dance leads with 26 plays, plus Digital Love, Veridis Quo, and Instant Crush. Discovery (2001) fuses mid-80s Kool and the Gang R&B with vocoders and post-millennial prog, and Veridis Quo is its ambient heart — a rare instrumental moment of cinematic stillness. The collaboration web runs deep: Thomas Bangalter's side project Stardust (with Alan Braxe) produced the era-defining 'Music Sounds Better With You'; their former Darlin' bandmate Laurent Brancowitz went on to found Phoenix; they co-produced four tracks on Kanye West's Yeezus; Nile Rodgers and Pharrell Williams anchored Random Access Memories; and their final production was Parcels' 'Overnight' in 2017. Their manager Pedro Winter (Busy P) founded Ed Banger Records, launching Justice — the clearest sonic heir to their French house legacy.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Glenn Gould
play_commands.album: Scarlatti: Sonata in G Major, K. 13
play_commands.narrative: Glenn Gould's 1968 recording of Scarlatti's Sonata in G Major, K. 13 comes from his Renaissance & Baroque collection on Columbia, where Gould applies his signature crystalline touch to a composer born the same year as Bach and Handel. Scarlatti spent his creative life far from the German mainstream, composing 555 keyboard sonatas at the Spanish and Portuguese courts that fused Italian virtuosity with Iberian folk rhythms. Gould's piano reading emphasizes the sonata's contrapuntal clarity, offering a distinctly different perspective from the harpsichord tradition championed by Scott Ross and Pierre Hantaï.

suggestions.genre_source: He is classified primarily as a Baroque composer chronologically, although his music was influential in the development of the Classical style. Baroque composer of 555 keyboard sonatas.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Bobby Timmons
play_commands.narrative: Bobby Timmons brought Philadelphia church music into the heart of hard bop — his gospel-drenched piano defined Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers in the late '50s, where he wrote "Moanin'" and "Dat Dere," two of the most iconic soul jazz compositions ever recorded. Soul Time, recorded in August 1960 for Riverside under producer Orrin Keepnews, pairs Timmons with Blue Mitchell's lyrical trumpet and the rhythm section of Sam Jones and Art Blakey himself — the same powerhouse engine from the Messengers. When Timmons left to lead his own trio, Cedar Walton took the piano chair, and Timmons's earlier stint with the Cannonball Adderley Quintet had already produced the classic "This Here."

play_commands.title: Exploring: Les Arts Florissants
play_commands.narrative: Haydn's Harmoniemesse (1802) is his last completed major work — a valedictory masterpiece composed at seventy for the name-day of Princess Esterházy, pouring a lifetime of symphonic mastery into the grandest wind-band scoring of any of his masses. William Christie and Les Arts Florissants bring their celebrated French Baroque sensibility to this Viennese Classical summit in a brand-new 2026 recording on Harmonia Mundi, a fascinating meeting of period-practice traditions. BBC Radio 3's Building a Library with Richard Wigmore chose Sigiswald Kuijken and La Petite Bande as the benchmark recording — making this new Christie version a compelling counterpoint.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Air
play_commands.narrative: La femme d'argent opens Moon Safari with a seven-minute groove built on a Can sample from Future Days — Nicolas Godin and Jean-Benoît Dunckel self-produced the album at their own studio with early production input from Étienne de Crécy on the pre-Air single 'Modular Mix.' The Versailles duo sit at the center of a web connecting Phoenix (Thomas Mars sang on The Virgin Suicides score as 'Gordon Tracks'), Charlotte Gainsbourg (Air wrote and played every note on her album 5:55), Beck (who guested on 10 000 Hz Legend), Nigel Godrich (who co-produced Talkie Walkie, fresh off Radiohead's Amnesiac and Hail to the Thief), and Sofia Coppola, whose three films all feature Air music.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Liz Phair
play_commands.narrative: Soap Star Joe is the snarling opener of Exile in Guyville, Liz Phair's 1993 debut that was essentially a two-person project — Phair wrote every song and Brad Wood produced, engineered, and played drums on every track. Wood went on to produce Phair's next three albums (Whip-Smart, Whitechocolatespaceegg, Soberish) plus landmark records for Veruca Salt, Sunny Day Real Estate, Tortoise, Smashing Pumpkins, and Pete Yorn — a thread that runs through the entire '90s Chicago/indie scene. Casey Rice engineered alongside Wood at Idful Studios; the album was famously structured as a track-by-track response to the Rolling Stones' Exile on Main St.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Donald Byrd
play_commands.narrative: Donald Byrd is a first listen — no prior plays in the library. "My Girl Shirl" comes from Byrd In Flight (1960), an early hard bop session featuring Duke Pearson on piano. Byrd's story splits into two fascinating eras: the Blue Note hard bop years (late '50s–'60s) alongside Art Blakey, Lee Morgan, and Herbie Hancock, and the revolutionary jazz-funk period produced by Larry and Fonce Mizell starting with Black Byrd (1973) — which became Blue Note's all-time biggest seller. The Mizell Brothers connection opens a whole production web: they gave the same treatment to flutist Bobbi Humphrey (Blacks and Blues) and Byrd himself formed The Blackbyrds from his students at Howard University, passing the jazz-funk torch directly.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Hania Rani
play_commands.narrative: Hania Rani (Hanna Raniszewska) trained at the Chopin University in Warsaw and did postgrad work in Berlin before sending an unsolicited demo to Manchester's Gondwana Records — they wrote back the next day. Esja was recorded on two Yamaha pianos in her Warsaw flat and in Reykjavík, where she found Ólafur Arnalds' piano in engineer Bergur Þórisson's studio. Her collaboration web runs deep: cellist Dobrawa Czocher has been her partner since music school (White Flag, Inner Symphonies on Deutsche Grammophon), Ghosts features Arnalds on "Whispering House" and Duncan Bellamy of Portico Quartet, and she released a split single with Portico Quartet on their shared Gondwana label. An opera commissioned by Theatre Basel premieres in October 2026.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Aphex Twin
play_commands.narrative: Richard D. James has been reshaping electronic music from a Cornish bedroom since age 14 — Nanou2 lands on the tender, prepared-piano side of Drukqs, a sprawling 2001 double album that swings between brutal drill-and-bass and Satie-influenced Disklavier miniatures. James operates almost entirely solo but under a constellation of aliases (AFX, Caustic Window, Polygon Window, The Tuss), co-founded Rephlex Records, and sits at the center of Warp Records' IDM universe alongside Autechre, Squarepusher, and Boards of Canada. His one true collaboration album was Expert Knob Twiddlers with μ-Ziq (Mike Paradinas), and he once commissioned Philip Glass to orchestrate a track from ...I Care Because You Do — a collision of worlds that perfectly captures his range.

suggestions.note: Darker, more abstract sequel — inspired by lucid dreams and synaesthesia. Hit #11 in the UK despite polarizing critics. 24 untitled tracks of deep ambient immersion.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Maxwell
play_commands.narrative: Maxwell's Urban Hang Suite is where the neo-soul movement crystallized — recorded at Electric Lady Studios with songwriter Leon Ware (who co-wrote Marvin Gaye's 'I Want You') and guitarist Wah Wah Watson, plus Sade's Stuart Matthewman co-writing and co-producing three tracks. Maxwell (credited as Musze) also sang on Sweetback's 1996 debut, a side project by Sade's band members, cementing that Sade–Maxwell connection. Alongside D'Angelo and Erykah Badu, Maxwell helped define late-'90s neo-soul, and after an eight-year hiatus returned with BLACKsummers'night, which he co-produced with Hod David and won two Grammys.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Abel Selaocoe
play_commands.narrative: We've already explored Selaocoe's albums and his Giovanni Sollima and Yo-Yo Ma connections — this time let's follow the arranger thread. The Bach Sarabande you're hearing was arranged by Fred Thomas, a British multi-instrumentalist and ECM recording artist who has created bespoke arrangements for Selaocoe, Rachel Podger, and Hilary Hahn. Thomas's own Bach album Three or One reimagines organ chorale preludes for piano trio with cellist Lucy Railton — produced by Manfred Eicher for ECM — offering a fascinating parallel to Selaocoe's cross-cultural reimagining. Meanwhile, Manchester Collective, the string ensemble backing Selaocoe on this very track, recently premiered Hania Rani's piano concerto Non Fiction, and Selaocoe's regular percussion partner Bernhard Schimpelsberger has his own solo album Avenues blending Austrian tabla with electronic textures.

suggestions.note: Selaocoe's regular percussion collaborator (they perform together as Chesaba) — Austrian-born tabla player who studied in India, blending Hindustani rhythms with electronic production.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Abel Selaocoe
play_commands.narrative: Your first encounter with Abel Selaocoe — a South African cellist, vocalist, and composer who fuses Bantu throat singing and African percussion with Baroque cello repertoire. This Bach Sarabande arrangement (by Fred Thomas for cello & string orchestra) comes from his sophomore album *Hymns of Bantu* (2025, Warner Classics), where it sits alongside traditional South African hymns and Giovanni Sollima's *LBFiles* suite. Selaocoe trained at the Royal Northern College of Music in Manchester and collaborates regularly with Manchester Collective, percussionist Bernhard Schimpelsberger, and djembe player Sidiki Dembélé — and Yo-Yo Ma guests on his debut album *Where Is Home*.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Cleo Sol
play_commands.narrative: Cleo Sol's Rose in the Dark is where it all begins — her 2020 debut, entirely produced by her husband Inflo (Dean Josiah Cover), who also helms the mysterious UK collective SAULT and produced Michael Kiwanuka's Mercury Prize-winning KIWANUKA. Every Cleo Sol album lives on Inflo's Forever Living Originals label, making their partnership one of the most prolific artist-producer marriages in modern British soul. She's also featured on two Little Simz albums — "Selfish" on Grey Area (2019) and "Woman" on Sometimes I Might Be Introvert (2021), both also produced by Inflo — a triangle of London talent that keeps feeding itself.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Sade
play_commands.narrative: You're hearing Sade through The Neptunes' lens — Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo remixed 'By Your Side' for this 2011 compilation, bridging Sade's signature smooth soul with early-2000s beat science. The original track lives on Lovers Rock (2000), Sade's Grammy-winning fifth album that the band self-produced. What Spotify won't tell you: Sade's saxophonist Stuart Matthewman co-wrote and co-produced Maxwell's landmark Urban Hang Suite (1996), and the rest of the band formed Sweetback — a side project featuring Maxwell and Amel Larrieux that pushed Love Deluxe's electronic atmospherics even further. Their debut Diamond Life (1984) was produced by Robin Millar, who crafted that iconic warm-yet-precise sound.

play_commands.title: Exploring: Sigur Rós
play_commands.narrative: Hoppípolla pulled you into Sigur Rós — the Icelandic post-rock band built around Jónsi Birgisson's bowed guitar and falsetto vocals, active since 1994 out of Reykjavík. Takk... (2005) was self-produced by the band with engineer Ken Thomas, who also engineered their breakthrough Ágætis byrjun (1999) and the all-Hopelandic ( ) (2002). The production web fans out from there: Alex Somers (Jónsi's partner) co-produced their ambient masterpiece Valtari (2012) and collaborated with the band on Black Mirror's 'Hang the DJ' score, while their latest, ÁTTA (2023), was produced with Paul Corley — the same producer behind Ben Frost's and Oneohtrix Point Never's records. Jónsi's solo work and his ambient project with Somers (Riceboy Sleeps) extend the sonic world, and Amiina, the Icelandic string quartet who toured with Sigur Rós for years, released their own gorgeous debut Kurr in 2007.

suggestions.label: 💿 Takk... (2005) — Sigur Rós

play_commands.title: Exploring: Boards of Canada
play_commands.narrative: Boards of Canada's Inferno is their first album in 13 years, breaking a silence that stretched back to 2013's Tomorrow's Harvest — and you're already in on it with 'Deep Time.' The Scottish brothers Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin are famously reclusive and self-produced on their own Hexagon Sun label/studio, but their remix and production web runs deep: they've remixed Beck's 'Broken Drum' (from Guero/Guerolito), cLOUDDEAD's 'Dead Dogs Two,' Boom Bip's 'Last Walk Around Mirror Lake,' and multiple tracks for Nevermen (the Tunde Adebimpe / Doseone / Mike Patton supergroup). They've also produced for The Sexual Objects and are deeply embedded in the Warp Records ecosystem alongside Autechre, Aphex Twin, and Bibio. Their 2019 Societas x Tape NTS Radio mix is a rare window into their own influences.
